passages.happening:
God tells Moses to speak to Aaron about the lamps: “When you set up the seven lamps, they are to light the area in front of the lampstand” (verse 2). Aaron does so.

“This is how the lampstand was constructed: it was made of hammered gold from its base to its blossoms, fashioned according to the pattern the LORD had shown Moses” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is about setting the Levites apart, and it begins, perhaps surprisingly, with a lamp. The placing is deliberate. First the light inside the holy place is set to shine. Then the people who will serve that holy place are made ready.

The lampstand is the menorah. It was hammered from a single piece of gold, with branches shaped like almond blossoms, after the pattern God had shown Moses on the mountain (Exodus 25:31-40). It stood in the outer room of the tent, the holy place. That room had no windows. The seven lamps were its only light, and the priests kept them burning.

Verse 2 gives one instruction: the lamps are to throw their light forward, into the room. A lamp exists to give light to what is in front of it.

The menorah became the best-known sign of the Jewish people. After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, a lampstand from its treasures was carried through Rome, and the scene is carved on the Arch of Titus, which still stands there.
passages.later:
Solomon's temple had ten lampstands, ‘five on the right side and five on the left’ (1 Kings 7:49).

In the temple courts Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

In Revelation John sees ‘seven golden lampstands’, and among them ‘One like the Son of Man’ (Revelation 1:12-13). He is told that the lampstands are the churches.
passages.asks: The lamps were set so that their light fell forward into the room. Ask where the light you have been given falls: on yourself, or on what is in front of you. And ask who is sitting in the dark within reach of you.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to make the Levites clean. They are sprinkled with water, they shave their whole bodies, and they wash their clothes (verse 7).

Then the whole congregation gathers. “You are to present the Levites before the LORD and have the Israelites lay their hands upon them” (verse 10). Aaron presents the Levites to God ‘as a wave offering from the sons of Israel’ (verse 11). The Levites in turn lay their hands on two bulls, which are offered for them (verse 12).

God gives the reason once more. “For the Levites have been wholly given to Me from among the sons of Israel” (verse 16). He has taken them in place of every firstborn son, and he gives them to Aaron as helpers (verses 18-19). It is all done ‘just as the LORD had commanded Moses’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 said that God had taken the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn. Chapter 4 gave them their loads. This chapter is the ceremony that sets them apart.

The washing uses Israel's ordinary signs of cleansing, in a strong form. Water, shaving and clean clothes were also required of a person healed of a skin disease (Leviticus 14:8-9). The Levites are made ready to come near holy things.

The most striking act comes next. Usually a worshiper laid his hand on the head of an animal he was offering, as a sign that it stood for him (Leviticus 1:4). Here the people lay their hands on the Levites. The whole nation is saying that these men stand for them.

Then the Levites are presented as a wave offering. A wave offering was usually a portion of food, lifted or moved before the altar to show that it was given to God, and then handed to the priests. Here the offering is a tribe of living men. They are given to God on behalf of the nation, and God hands them to Aaron and his sons as their helpers. Nowhere else in the Old Testament are people called a wave offering.

The chapter's words mark a difference between Levites and priests. The priests were anointed with oil and consecrated (Leviticus 8:12). The Levites are cleansed. Their service is real and near, but it is not the priests' service.

Verse 19 states what the Levites are for. They serve at the tent on Israel's behalf, ‘so that no plague will come against the Israelites when they approach the sanctuary’. Their place between the tent and the tribes is a protection for everyone.
passages.later:
Paul uses the picture of a living offering for every believer: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).

The laying on of hands became the church's way of setting people apart for service. When seven men were chosen in Jerusalem to care for the widows, the apostles ‘prayed and laid their hands on them’ (Acts 6:6).
passages.asks: A whole tribe was offered to God alive, and then put to work. Ask what it would mean to think of your own ordinary week, your body and your hours, as an offering already given. And ask who serves on your behalf in ways you have never thanked them for.

passages.t: Years of service, and what comes after
passages.happening:
God sets the years of a Levite's work. “Men twenty-five years of age or older shall enter to perform the service in the work at the Tent of Meeting. But at the age of fifty, they must retire from performing the work and no longer serve” (verses 24-25).

Retirement is not the end of belonging. “After that, they may assist their brothers in fulfilling their duties at the Tent of Meeting, but they themselves are not to do the work” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a practical rule. The work of the Levites was heavy. It meant taking down a large tent, carrying it across a desert and putting it up again. The law gives that work to men in their strength and releases them from it at fifty.

The older men are not sent away. They may still assist their brothers. They set down the load and stay in the company of those who serve.

The starting age here is twenty-five. Chapter 4 counted Levites from thirty. Some interpreters see a time of training from twenty-five to thirty. Others think the two chapters reflect practice at different times. By David's reign the age had been lowered to twenty, because the tent no longer had to be carried (1 Chronicles 23:24-27).
passages.later: The Psalms pray for those who are past their strength: “Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails” (Psalm 71:9). And another psalm says of the righteous, “In old age they will still bear fruit” (Psalm 92:14).
passages.asks: At fifty a Levite laid down the heavy work and went on assisting his brothers. Ask whether you measure your worth, or anyone else's, by how much can still be carried. And ask what an older person near you could still give, if someone asked them.
